newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spanish bonds at record highs, more gains expected.
newsitem.headline: Spanish bonds at record highs, more gains expected.

text.p: Spanish government bonds or bonos hit record highs for the third day in a row on Tuesday and reduced the spread with 10-year bunds to 215 bp, but dealers seemed convinced the best was yet to come.
"What is going on is that people are getting more confident that a relatively tight budget will be approved," Jose Luis Alzola, economist with Salomon Brothers in London, said.
"That helps the long end of the curve because a prospect of a tight budget increases the possibility that Spain will be in the EMU, maybe not from the start, but very soon."

Bonds were also helped by a comment from Bundesbank board member Peter Schmidhuber that there should be a rethinking of the timetable for the launch of a single currency if fewer than six countries qualified at the beginning.

"This (comment) helped a lot because it changes the framework for the Spanish market," said a dealer with a U.S. investment house in Madrid. "The market perception is that we'll soon see a future contract at 105."
The December contract on the Meff bond futures market reached a record high of 104.18 on Tuesday.
"We are seeing a lot of buying from foreigners, both from the U.S. and from northern Europe," the dealer said.
The possibility the Bank of Spain could cut its official rate as soon as the beginning of October is pushing short-date bond prices up.
Merrill Lynch said in a report it expected a 25 bp cut for month-end or at the latest for early October.

Ten-year yields declined briskly to 8.30 percent, well below 8.50 percent, which seemed a strong resistance just a week ago. The spread over bunds shrank to 215 from 223 at Monday's close and dealers expected further reduction in the coming weeks.
"We can go very fast at the 200 basis points level," another dealer said. "There isn't any resistance."

Even the growing possibility that the U.S. Federal Reserve could raise its rates before end-September, a factor that caused some profit-taking late on Tuesday, could eventually support the Spanish market.
"In the end this is going to help the dollar and, on this side, support the non-core European bond markets," Alzola said.
A possible flood of money toward peripheral markets should put Spain in a favourable situation, one dealer said.
"We saw a very good number for August inflation and we do wait that Spanish CPI will break under the three percent level in the next spring," Antonio Migelanes, an economist with BBV in Madrid said.
August CPI showed a less than expected 0.3 percent rise.
The yield differential with Italian bonds, which was around 70 basis points last week, rose to 82 on Tuesday and could rise a lot more in the coming days, dealers said.
"We do expect a little bit of widening in this spread because Spain is closer than Italy to meeting the Maastricht requirements," Alzola said.
Bank of America's analysts agreed in a client report published recently.
"In the near term the outlook for Spanish bonds looks slightly better than the Italian one, though both markets are vulnerable to growing tensions surrounding the European budgets," the report said.
